title: Stop Writing Loops to Cut Up Lists and Strings: Use Slicing
excerpt: Use [start:stop:step] to take the first items, the last items, every other item or a reversed copy, with no loop needed.

headings.text: Slices Are Copies and Forgive Out-of-Range Limits
A Practical Example: File Names and Phone Numbers

html:
Sometimes you need only part of a text or a list: the first three characters of a code, the last four digits of a phone number, every second item in a list. You could write a loop for each of those. Slicing lets you describe the part you want in a single short line, using square brackets and colons.

Slicing works the same way on text (called a string), on lists like [1, 2, 3] and on tuples like (1, 2, 3). Programmers call all three sequences, meaning ordered collections, so learning slicing once pays off three times.

Indexes Come First

Every item in a sequence has a position number called an index. Counting starts at 0, and negative numbers count backwards from the end:

word = "Python"

print(word[0])
print(word[5])
print(word[-1])
print(word[-2])
P
n
n
o

What does a negative index mean? -1 is the last item, -2 the one before it, and so on. It saves you from calculating the length just to reach the end.

The [start:stop] Slice

A slice names a start position and a stop position, separated by a colon:

print(word[0:2])
print(word[2:5])
print(len(word[2:5]))
Py
tho
3

Why does word[0:2] give "Py" and not "Pyt"? Because the stop position is excluded: the slice runs from the start up to, but not including, the stop. A handy consequence is that, when both limits are inside the sequence, the length of the slice (found with len(), which counts the items) is simply stop - start, which is why word[2:5] has 3 characters.

Leaving Parts Out

Do you always have to write both numbers? No. If you leave out the start, the slice begins at the very beginning. If you leave out the stop, it runs to the very end:

print(word[:3])
print(word[3:])
print(word[:])
print(word[-3:])
Pyt
hon
Python
hon

The last line is a common pattern for "the last three items". And word[:], with both ends left out, takes everything; for a list that gives a full copy.

The Step

A third number sets the step: how many positions to move each time. In [::2] the empty start and stop mean "the whole sequence", and the 2 means "take every second item, starting from the first". It is useful on lists of numbers:

numbers = [10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60, 70]

print(numbers[::2])
print(numbers[1::2])
print(numbers[::-1])
print(numbers)
[10, 30, 50, 70]
[20, 40, 60]
[70, 60, 50, 40, 30, 20, 10]
[10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60, 70]

How do you reverse a list without changing it? A step of -1 walks backwards, so numbers[::-1] builds a new reversed list. The last line confirms the original was left untouched.

Slices Work on Tuples Too

Does everything above also work on tuples? Yes, and the result is a tuple:

coordinates = (1, 2, 3, 4, 5)
print(coordinates[1:4])
(2, 3, 4)

Slices Are Copies and Forgive Out-of-Range Limits

A slice of a list is a separate new list, so changing it (here part[0] = 99 replaces its first item) does not change the original:

part = numbers[1:3]
part[0] = 99
print(part)
print(numbers)
[99, 30]
[10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60, 70]

One more difference from plain indexing: a slice that goes past the end simply stops at the end, but a single index that does not exist is an error, called an IndexError.

print(word[2:100])
print(word[100])
thon
IndexError: string index out of range

The slice word[2:100] printed "thon" without complaint and then the single index word[100] raised an IndexError, because there is no character at position 100.

A Practical Example: File Names and Phone Numbers

Slices shine on everyday text. Suppose you want a file's extension, the name without its extension, and a masked phone number that only shows the last four digits:

filename = "report_final.pdf"
print(filename[-3:])
print(filename[:-4])

phone = "9876543210"
print("XXXXXX" + phone[-4:])
pdf
report_final
XXXXXX3210

Notice that filename[:-4] means "everything except the last four characters". Counting from the end means the code keeps working even when the file name changes length.

Get the Code

Every example in this lesson, with its output, is in a notebook on GitHub: PythonSlicing.ipynb.

Summary

  • An index picks one item; counting starts at 0, and negative indexes count from the end.
  • seq[start:stop] takes items from start up to but not including stop.
  • Leave out the start or the stop to go to the beginning or the end; seq[-3:] is the last three items.
  • seq[::step] skips items, and seq[::-1] gives a reversed copy.
  • Slices work on strings, lists and tuples; a list slice is a new list, and out-of-range limits never raise an error.
